title: Saving the World's Languages
intro: Thousands of the world's languages could disappear this century, but some communities are showing that a language in danger can be brought back to life.

passage: Nobody knows exactly how many languages there are in the world, but most experts put the number at around 7,000. However, these languages are not shared equally. More than half of the world's population speaks just over twenty of them, including Chinese, English, Spanish and Hindi. At the same time, thousands of languages have fewer than 1,000 speakers, and many of these are now endangered, which means they may disappear completely within a few generations.

A language usually dies slowly. The process often begins when parents decide that their children will have a better future if they speak the dominant language of the country, the one that is used in schools, in business and on television. The children grow up understanding their parents' language but rarely speaking it, and the next generation may not understand it at all. When the last elderly native speakers die, the language goes with them.

Why should this matter? Many linguists argue that every language is a unique way of seeing the world. Some languages have detailed words for local plants, animals and weather that contain knowledge built up over hundreds of years. For example, the names that a community uses for plants may show which ones can be used as medicine. When a language is lost, this knowledge can be lost too. For many people, their language is also an important part of their identity and connects them to their history.

Fortunately, the story does not always end badly. Hebrew is perhaps the best-known example of a language that has been revived. For centuries it was used mainly for religious texts and prayers, and it was not anyone's first language. From the late nineteenth century, however, a group of enthusiasts began to use it at home and in schools. Today it is an official language of Israel and is spoken by millions of people.

Smaller languages can be saved too. In New Zealand in the 1980s, Māori communities set up 'language nests', where young children spend the day with fluent older speakers and hear only Māori. The idea has since been copied in other places, including Hawaii, where a similar programme helped to increase the number of young people who speak Hawaiian. In Wales, the Welsh language is taught in schools and appears on road signs, and there is a Welsh-language television channel.

Technology is also helping. Linguists now use digital recorders and video cameras to preserve the voices of the last speakers, and some endangered languages have their own apps and online dictionaries. However, experts agree that recordings alone cannot keep a language alive. A language only survives if people use it in daily life and pass it on to their children. Saving a language takes a great deal of effort, but for the communities involved, it is worth it.

mcq.q: Why do some parents stop speaking their own language to their children?
options: Their children refuse to learn it at school.
They think the dominant language will give their children a better future.
The government does not allow it to be used at home.

mcq.q: According to paragraph C, what can the plant names in some languages show?
options: Which plants can be used to treat illness.
Which plants are in danger of disappearing.
How old a community's traditions are.

mcq.q: What is the writer's view of technology in paragraph F?
options: It is the best way to save endangered languages.
It has made language nests unnecessary.
It is useful, but people must still speak the language.
